title: Nonprofit Workflow Automation Software: 2026 Guide
summary: Nonprofit workflow automation software moves donor and volunteer data between systems automatically. See which options fit your nonprofit.
body_markdown:
## 2. Zapier and Make for non-technical nonprofit teams


If staff or a part-time volunteer, not an IT department, will own the workflows, Zapier and Make fit, and unlike Power Automate their prices are published.


Charity surveys on IT support show most small nonprofits lean on outsourced help or volunteers, so a tool that someone can fix without writing code matters more than how many apps it connects to.


Because both Zapier and Make are hosted services, donor data passes through the vendor's cloud, with no self-hosted option. That settles the second question early.


### Zapier for staff-run teams


Open a Zapier automation and it reads as a linear chain: a trigger, then actions. A development officer can read one top to bottom and see what it does, so a handover to the next person is a short conversation rather than a code review.


There is a free plan, but it limits volume and keeps multi-step workflows out of reach. Anything beyond a single "new form entry, add a row" flow pushes you onto a paid plan.


**15% is the discount Zapier gives nonprofits** , making their platform pricing more attractive to these organizations.


On annual cost, Professional falls from $239.88 to $203.90, and Team from $828 to $703.80, meaning the discount compounds into material annual savings.


The discount saves about $36 a year on Professional and about $124 on Team, so Team tier deployments unlock substantially greater annual savings for nonprofits.


What does change the bill is metering. Zapier counts usage in tasks, one for each action a workflow completes, so a ten-step workflow that runs on every donation uses far more of your allowance than a two-step one.


Before you commit, count the steps in your busiest workflow and multiply by your monthly volume.


### Make for visual workflows


On a Make canvas, workflows appear as connected modules, with branches, filters and loops visible on screen. For a team that wants to route a gift differently by amount, campaign or donor type, that picture is easier to reason about than a long chain.


Expect a steeper first week: staff who have never seen a flowchart-style builder will need time to get comfortable.


On Make's free plan usage is capped, and it meters by operations, meaning each module that runs counts, not each finished workflow. A branching scenario that touches many modules per record can use up an allowance faster than its simple appearance suggests.


I haven't put a nonprofit discount figure here because I couldn't confirm one, so ask Make directly before assuming one applies.
